A LOC video track has two instances. Instance 0 covers every reference frame with a 200 ms span, three repair layers and a symbol track for datagram delivery. Instance 1 covers key frames only, with a 1000 ms span. Non-reference frames belong to no instance and are unprotected.
section.sourcecode: { "version": 1, "tracks": [ { "name": "video", "packaging": "loc", "isLive": true, "codec": "av01.0.08M.08", "width": 1920, "height": 1080, "framerate": 30, "bitrate": 4000000, "fec": [ { "instanceId": 0, "scheme": "reed-solomon", "blockProfile": "moq-object-v1", "sourceSymbols": 200, "symbolSize": 1100, "repairSymbols": 8, "interleaveDepthMs": 200, "reorderToleranceMs": 40, "repairTrack": "video/r0", "symbolTrack": "video/s0", "label": "reference frames" }, { "instanceId": 1, "scheme": "reed-solomon", "blockProfile": "moq-object-v1", "sourceSymbols": 180, "symbolSize": 1100, "repairSymbols": 24, "interleaveDepthMs": 1000, "repairTrack": "video/kf", "label": "key frames" } ] }, { "name": "video/s0", "packaging": "fec-source", "isLive": true, "source": "video", "instanceId": 0, "priority": 128 }, { "name": "video/r0", "packaging": "fec-repair", "isLive": true, "source": "video", "instanceId": 0, "repairLayer": 0, "repairSymbols": 8, "priority": 240 }, { "name": "video/r1", "packaging": "fec-repair", "isLive": true, "source": "video", "instanceId": 0, "repairLayer": 1, "repairSymbols": 16, "priority": 244 }, { "name": "video/r2", "packaging": "fec-repair", "isLive": true, "source": "video", "instanceId": 0, "repairLayer": 2, "repairSymbols": 16, "priority": 248 }, { "name": "video/kf", "packaging": "fec-repair", "isLive": true, "source": "video", "instanceId": 1, "priority": 236 } ] }
section.t: From this a receiver derives, for instance 0: O_0 = 0, O_1 = 8, O_2 = 24, total P = 40, so RSB_length is 40 on every repair object of the instance; layer 1 carries RS_IDs 8 to 23 and layer 2 RS_IDs 24 to 39. A full block has K + P = 240 symbols. A receiver holding layers 0 and 2 tolerates the loss of 24 symbols per block, minus the scheme's decoding overhead.

A key frame belongs to both instances, so its FEC Source Info Property carries two entries, for example 00 00 00 1F 40 01 00 00 03 E8: SS_ID 8000 in instance 0 and SS_ID 1000 in instance 1. A predicted frame belongs to instance 0 only, so it carries the 4-byte form, its SS_ID in instance 0; a non-reference frame carries no FEC Source Info Property.

A receiver on a clean path subscribes to "video" only. One on a lossy path with a tight deadline subscribes to "video/s0" over datagrams and "video/r0", adds "video/r1" when blocks fail, and adds "video/kf" if key frames are still lost. The two instances share T = 1100, so the key-frame symbols it receives on "video/s0" can also count toward instance 1 (Section 8.4). Each relay forwards all of these without knowing what they are.

section.name: Priority and Congestion
section.t: Priorities use the MoQ Transport scale : an 8-bit value in which a numerically lower value is delivered first. Repair tracks SHOULD have a numerically greater Publisher Priority than the source data they protect, so that repair is shed first under congestion, and the layers of an instance have non-decreasing priority values with layer index (Section 10.3, rule 10), so that the highest layer is shed first and a receiver degrades through its layers in order. The RECOMMENDED assignment places a repair track's priority value at least 64 above its source track's (e.g. repair 240 against a source track at the common default of 128):

tr.td: Repair of a more important class

section.t: A repair track's configured priority is the Publisher Priority of all its objects; a publisher conveys it, for example, with the track's DEFAULT_PUBLISHER_PRIORITY ( Section 10.4). Subscriber priority is applied before publisher priority, so a receiver SHOULD NOT subscribe to a repair track with a numerically lower subscriber priority than its subscription to the data that the repair protects.

MoQ Transport priorities apply to objects whatever their delivery mode, but implementations differ in how they schedule QUIC datagrams against stream data: some send all pending datagrams before any stream data, others send them after. A publisher that sends source data on streams and repair as datagrams on the same connection therefore cannot rely on priority alone to keep repair from delaying source, or source from delaying repair. Keeping the families of Section 6.4 apart avoids the interaction, and spreading each block's emission over its span (Section 9.3) reduces it. A publisher keeps repair from delaying its source on such a hop by sending a block's repair objects only after it has sent the block's source objects.

Repair adds load. On a path whose loss comes from congestion, rather than from the channel, repair that a receiver adds competes for the bottleneck that is dropping its packets. This is why a receiver SHOULD take its capacity into account before adding repair (Section 7.4), and why the layers of an instance are shed in order under congestion.

section.name: Relay Considerations
section.t: Relays need not implement FEC. Repair tracks and symbol tracks are ordinary tracks, and the FEC Source Info and FEC Unit Start Properties are ordinary Properties. The mechanism nevertheless relies on relays doing a few simple things well, and a relay that does not do them prevents FEC, or part of it, for the tracks it serves:

ol.li: Forward every object of a Group, including Groups delivered as datagrams. A symbol or repair Group holds many objects. A relay that forwards only one object per datagram Group delivers one symbol per block. A publisher whose receivers sit behind such a relay can send repair objects on streams, which carry every object's Object ID; a symbol track has the same option (Section 6.2).
Do not alter Immutable Properties. forbids it. A relay that alters them changes the Protected Object Unit and silently corrupts recovery of the other objects of the block.

Cache repair and symbol objects and answer FETCH for them, whatever their delivery mode. Fetching a block's repair or symbols from a nearby cache is the per-block recovery of Section 7.7. A relay that refuses FETCH for objects that arrived as datagrams leaves receivers only the choice of subscribing to more layers.

Do not assume contiguous Group IDs. Repair and symbol Group IDs are sparse (Section 7.6). Within each such Group, Object IDs start at 0 and are contiguous, so a cache that expects Object 0 in every Group serves these Groups.
Apply MoQ Transport priority to objects sent as datagrams as to objects sent on streams.

Withdraw an upstream subscription promptly when its last downstream subscriber leaves. A receiver drops a repair layer to save its own bandwidth, and the saving reaches the links above the relay only when the relay unsubscribes upstream.

section.t: A relay MUST NOT forward an object that it rebuilt by FEC as an object of the source track (Section 9.2). An entity that recovers objects and republishes them is a publisher of a new track.

section.name: LOC
section.t: A rebuilt object has only its Immutable Properties (Section 9.2), and a receiver that takes a symbol track receives every object as a rebuilt object (Section 6.2). On a LOC track , whose public metadata travels in Object Properties, a Property is recovered only if it is inside Immutable Properties. A publisher of a LOC track protected under "moq-object-v1" MUST carry inside Immutable Properties every LOC Property that it sets on a source object and that a receiver needs to decode or present the object, including Timestamp and Timescale and, where the track uses them, Video Config, Video Frame Marking and Audio Config. already recommends Immutable Properties for these. LOC Private Properties travel in the object payload and are recovered with it.

section.name: CMAF
section.t: On a CMAF track , each object holds one or more CMAF chunks, and the sample timing that a receiver needs is in each chunk's movie fragment, inside the payload, so a rebuilt object is complete without Properties. The CMAF header that initializes decoding comes from the catalog ( Section 3.1), not from the objects. Each object forms one Protected Object Unit. The publisher chooses K and T so that K x T covers the largest object, which for a chunk that holds a whole key frame can be large; for such objects symbol carriage, or a protection class of its own, avoids one lost object erasing more symbols than the block's repair covers.

A publisher can also close blocks at segment boundaries and choose a segment duration equal to the block span, so that a segment holds whole blocks; an entity serving HTTP Adaptive Streaming clients can then recover segments before it serves them.

section.name: Other Packagings
section.t: A packaging whose objects need information outside their Immutable Properties and payload to be decoded cannot be protected under "moq-object-v1" by symbol carriage, and loses that information for objects recovered under object carriage. Such a packaging, or one whose natural unit of protection is not a MoQ object, such as MMTP packets, needs a block profile of its own (Section 15.3), as Section 7.1 defines for MMTP packets.

section.name: Confidentiality
section.t: FEC provides no confidentiality. Source and repair symbols are computed over the bytes as transmitted, so when payloads are encrypted the symbols are computed over ciphertext and reveal nothing about the plaintext beyond what the ciphertext reveals (Section 8.6). The FEC Source Info Property, which must be readable without keys, reveals which instances an object belongs to; when instances follow frame classes, it reveals which objects are, for example, key frames. Object sizes and positions within Groups usually reveal as much. A deployment for which this matters uses a single instance. The FEC Unit Start Property reveals each object's size rounded up to whole symbols, which object carriage reveals exactly.

section.name: Integrity
section.t: An attacker who can modify or inject symbols can make a receiver rebuild incorrect objects. QUIC protects each hop, so on a MoQ path this requires a compromised relay. The checks of Section 9.2 discard many corrupt rebuilds but not all, and a decoder given a wrong symbol yields wrong source symbols without reporting an error; a receiver that decodes from exactly SSB_length symbols cannot detect it from the code. A receiver that holds more than SSB_length + e symbols of a block can re-encode the recovered block and compare the result with the symbols it did not use. End-to-end authentication of objects, such as MoQ Secure Objects, lets a receiver verify a rebuilt object as it verifies a received one (Section 8.6), which detects a corrupt rebuild.

Block signaling (SS_Start, SSB_length, RSB_length, and the PRIOR_GROUP_ID_GAP Property) is not authenticated end to end by this document. A compromised relay that injects a repair object with a false SSB_length, accepted before the genuine ones, can mis-delimit a block or cause the genuine repair objects to be discarded as inconsistent (Section 5.4). The effect is a block that fails to recover, not wrong media, when objects are authenticated end to end. The FEC Unit Start Property (Section 6.2) is likewise unauthenticated when carried among mutable Properties, which a relay may alter. A false Property starts the walk of Section 9.2 at a symbol that is not a unit start, or gives a unit a wrong s(o); the checks of Section 9.2 then reject the unit, or end-to-end authentication rejects what they pass, so the effect is a unit that fails to rebuild, not wrong media. A stripped Property costs only the partial rebuild, because a receiver does not infer from its absence that a symbol is not a unit start.

section.name: Resource Consumption
section.t: A receiver MUST NOT read, copy or allocate beyond the run it walks on the strength of a rebuilt length (Section 9.2). The configuration bounds the memory of one open block, (K + P) x T bytes, and the receiver bounds the number of open blocks (Section 9.4). A scheme's specification states the cost of decoding a block (Section 4.2), and a receiver MAY decline FEC for an instance whose cost exceeds its limits.

section.name: Amplification
section.t: Repair is additional traffic. Layering changes the amplification exposure, because the lever is which layers a receiver can be made to receive. A receiver receives only the repair tracks it subscribes to, so a relay or publisher MUST NOT deliver a repair or symbol track that a receiver did not subscribe to, and MUST NOT raise the repair count of a track that a receiver already holds as a way of raising its protection. Publishers MUST NOT generate excessive repair symbols that could be used for bandwidth amplification attacks. Publishers SHOULD keep the repair of layer 0 to a modest fraction of the source, for example P_0/K at most 50%. Each layer i adds P_i x T bytes per block, so deployments SHOULD bound the number of repair layers of an instance that any single receiver may hold, and SHOULD apply the same authorization to repair tracks as to the source tracks they protect.

section.name: MoQ Properties
section.t: This document requests two registrations in the "MOQ Properties" registry of (Section 8.4 of that document):

FEC_SOURCE_INFO is odd-typed because its value is bytes. 0x11, first requested by , lies in the range 0x00 to 0x77, for which states a registration policy of Standards Action or IESG Approval. That policy is not reachable by an individual draft, so this document asks for 0x11 as a provisional registration in the table maintains for other active drafts in the MoQ working group, on the same terms as the existing entries for draft-ietf-moq-loc and draft-ietf-moq-secure-objects, contingent on this document being adopted. If 0x11 is not available on those terms, an odd value in the range 0x80 to 0x37FF, whose policy is Specification Required, is obtainable by this document on its own. It costs at most one additional byte per tagged object, because Property types are delta-coded ( Section 8.3) and the extra byte appears only when the encoded Delta Type exceeds 127; it changes nothing else in this specification. FEC_UNIT_START is even-typed because its value is an integer. It is requested as TBD1, an even value from the range 0x80 to 0x37FF, whose policy is Specification Required and which this document can reach on its own; it is not requested from the provisional table, so its registration does not depend on adoption, and Section 6.2 refers to it by name until IANA assigns the value. Both Properties have Object scope: each describes the object it tags and carries no track-wide meaning. The even value 0x10 is not requested for FEC_SOURCE_INFO: it is the TIMESTAMP Property of , at Object scope in the same Property Type space (Section 5.6).
This document requests no MoQ control message type.

section.name: MoQ FEC Schemes Registry
section.t: This document requests a "MoQ FEC Schemes" registry in a new "Media over QUIC (MoQ) Forward Error Correction" registry group. A registration gives an Identifier, a string that no other entry uses and that the scheme parameter of Section 10.1 carries; a Class, "block" or "window"; whether the scheme supports repair layers; and a Reference. New registrations require Specification Required ( Section 4.6). The designated expert checks that the specification establishes each requirement of Section 4.2 for a block scheme, or of Section 4.3 and the document that completes it for a window scheme, includes test vectors, and states whether the scheme supports repair layers. This document registers no scheme; the block-codes companion document makes the first registrations, "reed-solomon" and "raptorq" (Section 12 of ). The Identifier "none" is reserved and MUST NOT be registered: it names no scheme, and companion documents use it where an encoding has to state that a track has no FEC instance ().

section.name: MoQ FEC Block Profiles Registry
section.t: This document requests a "MoQ FEC Block Profiles" registry in the same registry group. A registration gives a Block Profile string that no other entry uses, the source packagings it admits, and a Reference. New registrations require Specification Required. The designated expert checks that the specification fixes what Section 5.2 requires of a block profile. The initial content is:

tr.td: any packaging whose objects carry their media as whole MoQ objects, including loc and cmaf

section.name: Changes from draft-ramadan-moq-fec-01
section.t: This section is informative.

ul.li: The document no longer specifies an FEC code. Section 4 states the properties a scheme must have; Reed-Solomon and RaptorQ move to , which designates Reed-Solomon as mandatory to implement and RaptorQ as optional (Section 4.4).
The "moq-object-v1" construction is kept unchanged and is no longer limited to loc and cmaf.

Symbol carriage is new (Section 6.2): a symbol track whose objects are single source symbols, grouped by block, with Group ID ext(SS_Start) and Object ID equal to the ESI. It makes one lost datagram erase one symbol, and makes a block's source symbols fetchable by Group.

FEC instances are generalized (Section 5.1). The FEC Source Info Property can name several instances (Section 5.6), which gives protection classes and overlapping instances (Section 8) without reading payloads. The keyframe overlay, which relied on MMTP fields, becomes a special case of overlapping instances; its MMTP form moves to the MMTP block profile. An object whose only instance is instance 0 carries the 4-byte form, so that a set of instances has one encoding; a single Instance Entry naming instance 0 is malformed. A receiver of draft-ramadan-moq-fec-01 accepts only the 4-byte form and closes the session with KEY_VALUE_FORMATTING_ERROR on the list form; it interoperates only with tracks every tagged object of which belongs to instance 0 alone.

The FEC Source Info Property is now required to be inside Immutable Properties, where draft-ramadan-moq-fec-01 only recommended it, and must not be carried inside an encrypted container (Section 5.6). A malformed value closes the session only when a received object carries it; in a rebuilt object it fails the checks of Section 9.2 (Section 5.6 and Section 9.2).
Rebuilt objects can be placed in every instance they belong to (Section 8.4).

The configuration is defined as a data model (Section 10); its catalog encoding moves to . A track may declare several instances. The "none" algorithm of -01 Section 5.1 is dropped: a track without FEC declares no instance, and the binding states how a catalog expresses an empty instance list. The packaging values "fec-repair" and "fec-source" are registered by the binding, not here (-01 Section 15.3).

interleaveDepthMs is positive or absent unless a block profile gives zero a meaning of its own (Section 10.1); the ISO packet-count meaning of zero belongs to the MMTP block profile ( Section 7.1). Under "moq-object-v1" a zero value is a validation failure (Section 10.3, rule 11), where -01 Sections 5.1, 8.4 and 9 treated it as equivalent to an absent value.
Relay considerations are new (Section 12). Relays need not implement FEC, but the document does place a few requirements on them (Sections 3.2, 7.2, 12 and 14.4).
Section 7.2 adds a rule that -01 Section 6.2 did not have: a receiver should start a new repair subscription no earlier than the Group of the block in progress.
MMTP, ATSC 3.0, ARIB and multicast material moves to companion documents (Appendix A).

section.t: The following rules of draft-ramadan-moq-fec-01 were restored or changed by the editorial pass that produced this revision:

ul.li: Section 2 defines RSB_length, which -01 Section 2 did not define, by restating the field definition of -01 Section 7.1; Section 1.2 and Section 8.5 expand CMAF and LOC on first use, as the abstract of -01 did.
Section 4.3 lists, as item 6, what a sliding-window scheme must define for symbol carriage, which Section 6.2 states by block; symbol carriage no longer applies to such a scheme "unchanged".

Section 5.2: the mutable Properties, Subgroup ID, Publisher Priority and delivery mode are outside the unit, but a relay may change only the mutable Properties; -01 Section 7.6.1 never granted a relay more.
Section 5.6 reads 0x11 as provisional until the registration request is resolved and names the 0x80 to 0x37FF fallback and its 2-byte Delta Type consequence (-01 Section 5.3).
Section 6.2 records two open questions as Editor's Notes: whether the FEC Unit Start Property should exist, and whether PRIOR_GROUP_ID_GAP should be required on symbol-track objects.
Section 7.2 restores the recommendation of -01 Section 6.2 that a receiver subscribe to the source track, or to the instance's symbol track, before a repair track of the instance.
Section 7.3.1: the loss tolerance is derived and is not signaled as a separate parameter (-01 Section 6.3.2).

Section 7.3.2 restores the scope of -01 Section 6.3.9: a publisher applies a raised total from a block onward in serial order; the fail-closed check applies to a repair object of a held layer's own track, the layer being above 0, and to any held layer on a block at or after one that carried its O_i + P_i; such an object is not a symbol to discard; a larger RSB_length is not an error; and the backstop does not catch a withdrawal of the highest layer for a receiver that holds it alone. This section is the single normative statement of the check; the companions cite it. Section 7.5 defers to it for the RS_ID discard rule.
Section 7.5 restores the publisher-side bound on SSB_length of -01 Section 7.1: a publisher must not send 0 or a value above K; the receiver discard of such a repair object is stated in Section 5.4.
Section 7.7: a receiver that may not extend x has no range to request (-01 Section 7.5).
Section 9.2 rebuilds from each run of ESIs that no source object fed to the decoder covers, as -01 Section 7.6.4 did, so held-but-unfed objects keep their place in the run.

Section 9.3 carries the block and repair-Group figure and the typical-values table of -01 Section 9 as informative text; the deadline of a block whose first symbols were lost starts at the first signal from which the receiver learns of it, including an object of a successor block or a FETCH response (-01 Section 9); the reorderToleranceMs clauses of -01 Section 5.1 (finite, explicit zero distinct from absent, local policy kept separate, a deadline API that needs an allowance disables FEC without one) are carried; and Section 11 restores the remedy of -01 Section 10 for a hop whose stack does not apply Publisher Priority to datagram-delivered objects: a publisher sends a block's repair objects only after it has sent the block's source objects; Section 9.3 points at that rule and adds that the order holds within the block's span (new sentence); and, as -01 Section 9 did, Section 9.3 binds the publisher's send span and supplies an elapsed-time deadline only for a positive value, a zero value having only the meaning its block profile gives it (Section 10.1).

Section 9.4: a receiver must not discard a block before its deadline or while a FETCH for it is outstanding, except under a memory cap, and a block so discarded has reached its deadline unrecovered (-01 Section 9).
Section 10 keeps the three-sentence precedence rule of -01 Section 5.2: in-band signaling may exist, must not contradict the configuration, and is never required by a MoQ receiver.

Section 10.1: a receiver does not infer a block profile from the wire, and rule 1 of Section 10.3 requires the profile to admit the source track's packaging (-01 Section 5.1); a block profile may give interleaveDepthMs zero a meaning of its own; reorderToleranceMs is finite.

Section 10.2 and rule 10 of Section 10.3 restore -01 Section 6.3.4 rule 3: repair priorities are in 192 to 255, non-decreasing with layer index within an instance, and layer 0 defaults to 240; Section 11 points at the rule. Rule 9 points at the binding for the case of a catalog that declares no instance.

Rule 11 of Section 10.3 restores the scheme-neutral part of -01 Section 6.3.4 rule 13 as a fail-closed validation rule: sourceSymbols, symbolSize, the instance's repairSymbols and a repair track's declared repairSymbols are at least 1; the same rule holds the interleaveDepthMs zero check that Section 10.1 states. The scheme parts of rule 13 are in Section 7.

Section 11 restores the -01 Section 10 recommendation that a repair track's priority value is at least 64 above its source track's (repair 240 against a source track at 128), which the table alone does not state.
Section 10.4: a predicted frame carries the 4-byte form.

Section 12, item 1, restores the publisher remedy of -01 Section 7.5: a publisher whose receivers sit behind a relay that forwards only one object per datagram Group can send repair objects on streams, which carry every object's Object ID; the clause giving a symbol track the same option by way of Section 6.2 is new. The "at the time of writing" account of relay behaviour in -01 Section 7.5 is not carried (no implementations are named).
Section 14.2 names the FEC Unit Start Property as unauthenticated block signaling and states its effect.
Section 14.4 restores "publishers must not generate excessive repair symbols" and "deployments should bound the number of layers any single receiver may hold" (-01 Section 14.3).
Section 15.1 restores the range and policy facts of -01 Section 15.1 for 0x11, the Object-scope statement, and requests FEC_UNIT_START as TBD1 from the Specification Required range 0x80 to 0x37FF.
Section 15.2 registers no scheme; -01's "raptorq" and "reed-solomon" rows are requested by . The "Catalog Packaging Values" subsection is removed; requests those values.
Section 1.2, Section 5.2, Section 7.5, Section 10, Section 10.1, Section 10.2, Section 13.3 and Section 15.3 now name the companion documents where they take over.

Section 13.1 and Section 13.2 carry from -01 Section 7.6.5 that LOC Private Properties travel in the object payload and are recovered with it, and that the CMAF header that initializes decoding comes from the catalog, not from the objects.

, and carry the conformance cases of -01 Section 9, the worked example of -01 Section 7.6.7 and the message flows of -01 Appendix A.1, the last rewritten for "moq-object-v1" and the symbol track; its K and T are those of instance 0 of Section 10.4 (200 and 1100), not -01's 32 and 1312, which were sized for one MMTP packet per symbol and bound a unit to 41,984 bytes (Section 5.4), smaller than the key frame of . Section 3.2 restores the pointer of -01 Section 3 to the message flows.
Section 15.2 reserves the Identifier "none", which no scheme may take, so that the no-FEC encoding of stays distinct from every registered scheme.

Section 5.1 forbids reusing a symbol's coordinates across instances and feeding a symbol to another instance's decoder, except by the cross-instance placement of Section 8.4 at the SS_ID the unit's FEC Source Info Property gives it there.
Section 1.3 records as open that the MoQ Transport section cited in Section 15.1 for the "MOQ Properties" registry (-01 Section 15.1) is to be settled against the current MoQ Transport draft.

section.t: The questions this revision leaves open are marked [open] in the text: the registry pointer of Section 15.1 (Section 1.3); whether Section 4.3 holds for sliding-window schemes (Section 4.3); whether this document should itself require the mandatory-to-implement scheme (Section 4.4); and, in Section 6.2, whether the FEC Unit Start Property is worth its codepoint and whether PRIOR_GROUP_ID_GAP should be required on symbol-track objects.

section.name: Block Span Conformance Cases
section.t: This appendix is informative. These cases exercise the boundary rules of Sections 5.4 and 9.3 without deriving a block from a Group count. They use "iso-ssbg1-v1" ( Section 7.1), under which one source packet is one source symbol; works an example under "moq-object-v1".
The first case uses this numeric vector:

ol.li: A 30 fps track with a 30-frame (1000 ms) GOP may close a block after four access units (a four-frame access-unit interval). With the send schedule in the vector, interleaveDepthMs = 133. An access unit can produce multiple source packets, so the block is closed after those access units, not after an assumed packet count. For this concrete vector, the four access units begin at 0, 33.333, 66.667, and 100 ms, produce 2, 3, 1, and 4 source packets respectively, and therefore have SSB_length = 10 <= K = 16 as shown above. The publisher sends the last source or repair packet for that block by 133 ms; a later send would require a larger signaled window. The one MoQ Group containing the GOP can therefore contain several such blocks. Each repair packet still carries the actual (SS_Start, SSB_length); the 133 ms value does not mean four MoQ Groups per block and is not a rounded four-frame duration.

With K = 4, one Group containing three source packets followed by a Group containing three source packets may be encoded as blocks of lengths 3 and 3, or as a block of length 4 spanning the Group boundary followed by a block of length 2. Both are valid; the repair fields identify which partition was used.

If the stream ends with two source packets in the current block, the publisher sends a short block with SSB_length = 2, which under RaptorQ has the transfer length F = 2 x T ( Section 6.1), and no padding or skipped SS_ID. There is no following block.

section.name: Rebuilding a Block: Worked Example
section.t: This appendix is informative. It works the rebuild of Section 9.2 under object carriage, with the configuration in the catalog form of Section 10.4.

The configuration below declares a LOC video track under "moq-object-v1". Each one-second Group holds one Group of Pictures (GOP): an Instantaneous Decoder Refresh (IDR) frame as Object 0 and 29 P-frames as Objects 1 to 29 ( Section 4.2). The publisher sends the parameter sets in the IDR payload ( Section 2.1.1), so the track needs no Video Config.

Each object carries 15 bytes of Immutable Properties: Timescale in 4 bytes (Delta Type 0x08 and the value 90000 in 3 bytes), Timestamp in 5 bytes (a 4-byte value) and FEC Source Info in 6 bytes, the 4-byte form of Section 5.6. Each unit is therefore 37 bytes longer than its payload. With T = 1200:

ul.li: An IDR payload of 60,000 bytes gives len(o) = 60,037 and s(o) = 51. The unit's last symbol ends with 1,163 bytes of padding, which are not sent.
A P-frame payload of 7,000 bytes gives len(o) = 7,037 and s(o) = 6, with 163 bytes of padding.
A Group therefore spans 51 + 29 x 6 = 225 source symbols, within K = 256.

section.t: Suppose the first source object of the FEC instance, {0, 0}, has SS_ID 0, every Group so far has this shape, and the publisher closes a block at each Group boundary. Group g then starts at SS_ID 225 x g, and its block has SS_Start 225 x g and SSB_length 225. For Group 5:
Objects {5, 6} to {5, 28}, which the table omits, follow the same pattern.

Object {6, 0} starts at SS_ID 1350. The block's repair objects form Group 1125 of "video/repair" (Section 7.6): Objects 0 to 31, with RS_IDs 0 to 31 and ESIs 225 to 256, each 13 + 1200 = 1,213 bytes long. The block's source objects are sent over 967 ms, and its repair objects follow the last of them, so the instance's interleaveDepthMs of 1200 covers the block's send span (Section 9.3).

Suppose a delivery timeout drops {5, 3} and {5, 4}. The receiver holds {5, 2}, which ends at SS_ID 1187, and {5, 5}, which starts at SS_ID 1200, so ESIs 63 to 74 form a run of 12 missing source symbols. With the other 213 source symbols and the 32 repair symbols it holds 245 symbols, 20 more than SSB_length, and decodes. It walks the run from ESI 63. The unit there has Group ID 5, Object ID 3, Immutable Properties Length 15 and Payload Length 7,000, so len = 7,037 and s = 6, and bytes 7,037 to 7,199 from the start of the unit must be zero. The next unit, at ESI 69, is {5, 4} with s = 6, so the walk ends at ESI 75, where {5, 5} starts, as required. The FEC Source Info values in the two units are 1188 and 1194, their first SS_IDs. The receiver delivers both objects with their Timescale, Timestamp and FEC Source Info Properties.

This block recovers the loss of up to five P-frame objects, 30 symbols, with 2 symbols of decoding overhead, the overhead at which RaptorQ's residual failure is about 1e-6 (Section 4.2, requirement 7; Section 8). The IDR object spans 51 symbols, more than the block's 32 repair symbols, so its loss is not recovered in band: the receiver needs a further repair layer or a FETCH of the object, or resumes at the next Group.
This example uses "raptorq". Its configuration is not valid under "reed-solomon", since 256 + 32 exceeds 255 ( Section 7).

section.name: Example Message Flows
section.t: This appendix is informative. It shows the exchange of Section 3.2 for a track protected under "moq-object-v1", first under object carriage and then with the instance's symbol track.

section.name: Catalog-Driven FEC
section.t: The subscriber learns the complete FEC configuration from the track's catalog entry before subscribing, in the catalog form of Section 10.4:
section.artwork: Publisher Subscriber | | | (catalog obtained by SUBSCRIBE with | | request_id=0; fec field read) | | | | SUBSCRIBE(request_id=2, track=video, | | LOCATION_FILTER=0x05 (Next Object), | | FILL_PARAMETERS(LOCATION_FILTER= | | 0x01, StartGroup=1)) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | SUBSCRIBE_OK(LARGEST_OBJECT={G, n}) | |----------------------------------------->| | | | SUBSCRIBE(request_id=4, | | track=video/repair, | | LOCATION_FILTER=0x05 (Next Object)) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | SUBSCRIBE_OK | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Fill fetch stream: source objects | | {G, 0} to {G, n}] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Source objects from {G, n+1} on] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Repair objects, group=ext(SS_Start), | | obj=0..7] | |----------------------------------------->| | |
section.t: Each SUBSCRIBE carries a Request ID ( Section 6.4.2.1). A client uses even Request IDs, starting at 0 and rising by 2 per request, so the catalog SUBSCRIBE ( Section 5) takes 0 and the source and repair SUBSCRIBEs take 2 and 4. Each response travels on the bidirectional stream of its request, so SUBSCRIBE_OK carries no Request ID. The source subscription joins at the start of the current Group G ( Section 3.5). Its Next Object filter starts subscription delivery at {G, n+1}, where {G, n} is the Largest Object that SUBSCRIBE_OK reports, and its fill range, from {G, 0} to that Largest Object, arrives on a fill fetch stream. The repair subscription starts at the Next Object; repair objects published before it can be requested by FETCH (Section 7.7).

In this flow the track is a LOC track with a one-second Group duration. That Group duration describes the MoQ grouping; it does not derive an FEC block. For example, if the first block starts at SS_ID 0 and is full, its repair Group is its extended SS_Start, 0 (Section 7.6), the next block starts at SS_ID 200, and its repair Group is 200. A publisher may choose shorter blocks inside a Group or a block that crosses the Group boundary; each repair object carries the actual SSB_length. The subscriber's decoder configuration is derived from the configuration and each block's SSB_length (Section 4.2, requirement 5); no in-session message is required. The source objects carry the FEC Source Info Property of Section 5.6, and the repair objects are those of Section 7.5.

section.name: Symbol Carriage
section.t: A receiver that takes the FEC family of Section 6.4 subscribes to the instance's symbol track, "video/symbols", in place of or alongside the source track, with the same Next Object filter; its Request ID is the next even value.
section.artwork: Publisher Subscriber | | | SUBSCRIBE(request_id=6, | | track=video/symbols, | | LOCATION_FILTER=0x05 (Next Object)) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | SUBSCRIBE_OK | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Symbol objects as datagrams, | | group=ext(SS_Start), | | obj=0..SSB_length-1] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Repair objects, group=ext(SS_Start), | | obj=0..7] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | FETCH(request_id=8, track=video/symbols,| | LOCATION_FILTER=0x04 (Absolute Range),| | StartGroup=ext(SS_Start), | | the ESIs it lacks) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | [Fetched symbol objects] | |----------------------------------------->| | |
section.t: The symbol track's objects arrive as Groups whose Group ID is ext(SS_Start), the Group ID of the block's repair objects, with Object IDs 0 to SSB_length - 1 (Section 6.2); each datagram carries one symbol, so one lost datagram erases one symbol. A receiver that has lost symbols of a block and holds a repair or symbol-track object of it requests the symbols it lacks by a FETCH of the one Group ext(SS_Start) on the symbol track, or more repair from a layer it has not subscribed (Section 7.7). A receiver that takes only the symbol track and the repair layers receives the media as rebuilt objects (Section 9.2).
